A level on a list, or a source that does not exist, returns a 404 rather than a default sheet. The Back to grades button went with the move, since practice is no longer somewhere you arrive from grades, and the navigation now lists Practice beside the explorers rather than beneath one.

name: The card is not a button
summary: Every subject on an explorer sat inside one big control. The card was a button, and it holds buttons of its own - trouble, favourite, and the tick that chooses it - which is a control inside a control on four hundred and twenty-eight of them, one for every card on every list. What that costs is not theoretical. A screen reader announces the whole card as a single button and never reaches the favourite inside it, so the only way to mark a character as trouble is to see it. A keyboard arrives at the card and finds no way in. The glyph is the button now and the card is a plain container around it, which is the shape the saved lists and the history rows already used, so this is the odd one out being brought into line rather than a new idea. The controls at the glyph's foot are its neighbours instead of its children - the same corners, the same placement, nothing moved on screen - and each is reached, announced and pressed on its own. A whole card still answers a mouse click where it did before, because that is worth keeping and costs nothing once it is no longer the only way in.

name: All levels means all levels
summary: The WaniKani explorer offered a tab reading All with the total beside it - two thousand nine hundred and twenty-two - and pressing it did nothing you could see. It put the member back on their own level, which was the level already showing, so the list did not change, the address kept the same single level in it, and the number on the tab described a view nothing in the app could open. There was no way to look across every level at all. It selects every level now and fetches the ones it does not already hold, a few at a time rather than all at once, because a level that is not cached goes out to WaniKani and sixty of those together is how an account gets rate limited. Results widen as each batch lands instead of waiting for the last. The address carries the whole selection, so the long view is a link somebody can be sent. The subtitle went with it: it read Select one level at a time, which was true of nothing - Sticky has always let a member gather several - and it was the last thing still saying one.

name: A limit on signing up
summary: The route that creates an account had nothing bounding how often it could be called. It was never as bad as it sounds - a Google session is required before it does anything, and an address that already has an account gets that account back rather than a second one, so the ceiling was always one account per address rather than one per request. What was unbounded was the work behind it. Every call reads the signup settings, looks up the account, and scans every slug on the site to pick a free address, and a signed-in caller could repeat all of that as fast as they liked. Six attempts in ten minutes now, which leaves room for a form submitted twice, a retried request and a reload, and stops a loop. It is counted against the signed-in address rather than the caller's network address, because a household shares one of those - this one does - and a per-network budget would have the second person in a family turned away by the first. The check sits above all three reads rather than beside them, since a limit applied after the work bounds the answer and not the cost. None of this matters while the door is shut; all of it matters the moment it opens.

name: A list you can change your mind about
summary: A saved list was fixed the moment it was made. Renaming arrived a while back, so the label could be corrected, but what was actually in the list could not - taking one character out meant going back to an explorer, finding the other forty, choosing them all again and saving over the name. In practice nobody edited a list; they built a second one and left the first sitting there. Every list now has an Edit characters control beside Rename and Delete. The characters become the control rather than growing one beside them, because they are already the biggest thing on the card: tap one to take it out. Adding is a field you type into, since somebody who wants a particular kanji can type it faster than they can find it in a picker, and what is typed goes through the same tidying a saved selection does, so a pasted sentence and a chosen set reduce to the same thing. The whole edit is one save at the end rather than a request per character, which is one chance to go wrong instead of six. Emptying a list is refused: that is deleting it, and deleting has its own button and its own confirmation. While the panel is open the card's own preview and count stand aside, so there are never two different numbers on one card with nothing to say which is being changed.

name: The words the catalogue had missed
summary: Subject content is meant to come from the local catalogue rather than from WaniKani on every request - that is what makes the study queue quick. Ninety-eight subjects were not in it, so each one went out to the API instead, every time anybody's queue happened to include it. Almost all of them were the kana-only vocabulary a beginner meets first: これ, ホテル, おはよう, コーヒー, ありがとう. The reason was an interrupted sync months ago. A sync that stops keeps a cursor and a resumed run carries on from it rather than going back for what it skipped, so the gap stayed open and quietly widened as related words pointed at each other. There is a backfill for it now, and it is deliberately narrow: it works out what the app can ask for, subtracts what the catalogue holds, fetches only the difference, and inserts. It never updates and never deletes, because every row it writes was established as absent moments before - correcting content that is merely stale is the sync's job, and a tool that could overwrite is a tool that could lose something. It reports and writes nothing unless asked twice.

name: The practice chips work again
summary: Moving practice to /practice/jlpt/5 changed where the page reads its collection from and left every control on it still writing that collection into the query. Clicking G2, or WaniKani level 17, changed the address and nothing else: the page re-read a path that had not moved and rendered exactly what it was already showing. The link builder now produces the address the page actually reads - the collection in the path, and only how the sheet prints in the query - and a test asserts that what it writes parses back to what was asked for, which is the check that was missing rather than another eye on a screenshot. Building those links also dragged the server-only practice reader into the browser bundle, taking the page down with a 500, so the source names now live in a small module of their own with no database behind them. Verified by clicking the chips rather than by typing addresses, which is how the bug was found in the first place.

name: A selection survives the page turn
summary: Choosing items on an explorer kept its state in the component, and turning to page two is a navigation: the page remounted and took the selection with it - both the characters picked and the fact that picking was happening at all. Building a list of twenty across three pages is the ordinary way to do it, and it could not be done. The selection is now held for the sitting rather than for the component, under a key per surface so the grade explorer and the JLPT explorer do not overwrite each other. A session is the right span: a half-built selection is a task somebody is in the middle of, so it should survive a page turn and a stray reload without being handed back next week. Three links built from a selection still pointed at the practice sheet's old query-string address and did nothing when clicked - the same shape of break as the chooser chips, in the places that were not on screen when that was fixed.

name: Searching stays on the grade
summary: Searching from the grade explorer threw away both the grade you were on and the thing you searched for. Standing on grade three and looking for a character put you on grade one with an empty search box. The grade had recently moved out of the query string and into the path, which is the right shape - the path says which collection you are looking at, the query says how you are reading it - and the reader that used to take a grade out of the query was removed along with it. What was not looked at was the search form, which went on submitting to the collection root with the grade as a hidden field, the shape from before. The root reads no grade any more; it only opens the first one. The form posts to the grade own address now and carries nothing but the search. A guard test holds the shape, because this is the failure mode of changing an address: the thing itself gets changed and one caller does not.

name: The history table shows the character
summary: The admin study history listed twenty thousand answered reviews with a Subject column holding nothing but a number. A page of it read as a column of five figures, and there was no telling which row was about which character without looking every id up by hand - on the one screen whose whole job is reviewing what somebody answered. The character sits there now, with its id underneath in small type, because the id is still what the edit and delete actions act on and what a bug report quotes; it is just not the thing being read. The characters come from the local catalogue in a single query for the twenty or fifty rows a page actually shows, the same shape the table already used to turn account ids into names. A row whose subject the catalogue does not hold shows the id alone rather than a blank, since a subject can be answered and later withdrawn by WaniKani and the number is then the honest answer.

name: One top for every member page
summary: Study, the two explorers, Stats, News and Read are one page under six addresses, and each had grown a different top. Study and the explorers opened with a decorative banner and then kept their real title inside a filter panel that can be collapsed. Stats and Read had each built a header card of their own, similar but not the same. Read went further and put its Challenge and Check-ins toggle on a row above that card, so its heading sat a row lower than on any sibling - which is what made the set look less like one product the more of it you visited. There is one header now: a picture, the page name, a line saying what the page is for, and room on the right for what the page lets you do. The picture is per page, deliberately, because a page should still read as itself at a glance; the arrangement is not. The banner is gone from these six, the two private header cards are gone, and the toggle that used to push a heading down now sits below it with the rest of the content. What is still uneven, and is the next piece rather than a thing anybody should have to notice twice, is that the three explorers name themselves a second time inside their own panels.

name: The admin round
summary: Five things reported together, and one of them was hiding in every admin page rather than the one it showed up on. The release codename in the header refused to give up space, so on admin - ten tabs in the row beside it - it simply ran off the right edge and was cut in half; it shrinks and wraps to its own line now. Every admin page wrapped itself in a rule that clips anything reaching past its edge, which does nothing at all except cut off the user menu, and only looked like an Articles bug because Articles is short enough for the menu to reach past the bottom. The users table carried a filled button on every row labelled Open as user, which reads as impersonation: it is a plain link to the member's page, nothing is done as them, so it says View page and sits in the row menu with the other four actions instead of making the most ordinary thing look like the most consequential one. The signup settings laid three short choices out as three full-width bars on a screen over a thousand pixels wide, so the two questions could not be seen together; they are a grid. And the study history table listed twenty thousand answered reviews by subject id alone.

name: The selection shows what is in it
summary: The selection bar said twelve chosen and showed none of them, which is where a count stops being useful: you cannot tell whether the one you meant went in, whether a shift-sweep took one too many, or which of the twelve is the mistake, and the only remedy was to clear everything and start again. The chosen characters now sit in the bar as tags, each one removable by clicking it, so a wrong pick costs a click rather than the whole selection. Collapsed it is a single line ending in what is left over, since eighty characters would otherwise push the buttons off the screen, and the full set is one click away. Saving gained the other half of its job at the same time: it only ever made a new list, so building one across three sittings left three lists named almost the same thing. The lists that exist are offered first, each showing how many of the chosen it does not already hold, with naming a new one underneath. Adding is a union rather than a replacement, which is the difference between extending a list and emptying it.

name: Every admin header the same way
summary: Three admin pages drew their tab row as a band of their own underneath the header, while the other five put it inside the header beside the release name. Signup, Feature flags and a member's history were the three, so on those the codename sat above the tabs and everywhere else it sat beside them - the header changed shape as you moved between tabs of the same workspace, which is exactly the sort of thing that makes a set of pages feel unfinished without it being obvious why. The shared header has had a slot for this since the admin tabs were folded into it, and these three had simply never been moved across. They pass their tab row into that slot now, and all eight admin pages build their header the same way.

name: Lists you can actually manage
summary: The page is called Your lists and had no way to make one: every list had to begin as a selection on an explorer, saved under a name. That is one honest way to build a list and not the way somebody starts kanji I keep losing - they name the thing first and fill it as they meet them - so arriving here wanting to start one found nothing to click. There is a New list button on it now, and a list may be empty, which is what lets the naming come first; a list holding nothing says so rather than showing a blank strip. Emptying an existing list by editing is allowed for the same reason, since permitting an empty list to be created while refusing to empty one is a rule that holds in only one direction, and deleting is still its own button for being rid of the list rather than of its contents. The contents preview was set in the kanji accent at the card's heaviest weight, so a strip of thirty-five characters shouted over the name that identifies the list; the characters are what the card is about, but the name is what you scan for, so the preview is quieter and the name leads.

name: Read and News are real pages
summary: Six member addresses were not pages. Study, both explorers, Stats, News and Read all pointed at one file through a rewrite - the address bar said /users/john/read and the server was handed /users/john?dashboard=read - so the query string had not gone away, it had only stopped being visible. That is why those six had drifted into six different layouts without anybody editing six files, and it had a running cost: every one of them loaded every level snapshot on the account, each carrying that level's subjects, so opening Read to look at yen totals fetched seventeen levels of WaniKani data it would never show. Read and News are real pages now, with their own routes and their own loading. Read needs an account id. News needs the member's level. Neither needs anything else, and neither asks for it. The shared work - who is asking, whose page it is, whether they may see it - is one function rather than six copies. Stats and the three explorers are still on the old page and are the next to move.

name: A search outranks the filters it lands in
summary: Following a search result into an explorer landed in whatever that explorer was last left set to. Searching inu and clicking the dog arrived in a lesson-mode queue: of 157 matches it showed 2, and not one of the 34 kanji - the very character searched for among them. No filter on screen explained it, because the mode had been restored from the last visit rather than chosen, so it read as the search being broken. A search in the address now outranks the restored state: the queue mode, the tagged-list filter and the locked toggle are skipped rather than restored and then undone, which was a race the restore won about half the time. The searches you already ran also appear in the header dropdown, not only on the search page. It is the same component reading the same store on both, so an empty box offers the same thing wherever it is, and typing replaces them with suggestions as before.

name: Every member page is a page
summary: Six member addresses were not pages. Study, the WaniKani and JLPT explorers, Read, Stats and News were rewrites onto one component - the address bar said one thing and the server was handed the same file with a dashboard parameter, so the query string had never gone away, it had only stopped being visible. That is why those six drifted into six different layouts without anybody editing six files, and it had a standing cost: the shared file loaded every level snapshot on the account for all of them, so opening Read to read a table of yen fetched seventeen levels of WaniKani subjects it would never show. The three explorers were a second layer of the same thing, all three built at once with two hidden by stylesheet. Each of the six is a real route now and loads only what it shows. Read wants an account id. News wants the member's level. Only the JLPT explorer pulls the JLPT table and the member's kanji index, which used to be decided by a query parameter and is now decided by which page you asked for. The shared work is two loaders rather than one long file, the tab-switching component is gone because routing does that, and there are no rewrites left at all. A test holds the line, because a rewrite is the easy way to add an address and it is the wrong one: it buys a URL and skips the page.

name: One count, not two
summary: Searching the WaniKani explorer printed the answer twice. A line above the results said Showing 5 search results and the line on the toolbar said Showing 5 of 5 items - the same number, two sentences, neither of them wrong, and no way to tell whether they were counting the same thing or two different things that happened to agree. There is one count now, and a search changes what it says it is counting rather than adding a second opinion beside it: forty of sixty-nine items when you are browsing, five of five search results when you are searching.

name: One list layout
summary: The best list of subjects on the site was the one nothing could reuse. Choosing items in bulk opened a six-column table - item, reading, meaning, type, level, SRS - and it read better than every other list here, because a column of subjects is scanned one field at a time and that table was the only place the fields lined up. Everywhere else the reading sat squeezed under the meaning in a row that flowed to fit, so no two rows put anything in the same place. The table is gone and its shape is the shared list: study history, the study queue, the Trouble and Favourites lists and the bulk panel itself now draw the same lanes under the same headings, from one set of widths that the headings and the rows both read, so neither can drift from the other. On a phone the narrow lanes fold away and the reading returns under the meaning, because six columns do not fit in 393 pixels and a truncated reading is worse than a stacked one. Two things came with it: a row in the bulk list now removes its own item, where before picking one thing by mistake meant clearing all of them and starting over, and Select Visible works before anything is selected - it had been disabled until you had already chosen something by hand, which is the moment you least need it.

name: A result opens the thing it found
summary: Searching for 水泡 found it - Foam, vocabulary, level 46 - and selecting it opened the library explorer, which answered No item matched 水泡 about the word it had just been shown. The explorer was not being stubborn: it is built from the member's own levels and stops at theirs, so a member on level 17 has no level 46 for the word to appear in, and no filter would have helped. Results led to a list, and a list is free to answer with nothing. Words and radicals now have pages of their own, next to the kanji page that already existed, and every result leads to one: one subject, named in the path, showing its meanings, readings, the WaniKani explanation, the kanji it is built from or the kanji built from it, and example sentences that use it. They are public, because they describe a subject and not a member - which also ends the other half of this, where a signed-out reader got no link at all for a word or a radical and the row was dead text that looked like a link. Radicals are addressed by name rather than by glyph, since WaniKani draws a good number of them and those have no character to be addressed by. The address takes no viewer at all now, so a link copied out of a search works for whoever it is sent to.

name: Recent items, not recent searches
summary: The history remembered what you typed and forgot what you found. Search water, read down forty rows, open 水兵 - and what was kept was water. The question was recorded and the answer thrown away, which is backwards: the thing worth getting back to is the word, not the guess that led to it. Anything that opens a subject now adds to the list, from the results rows and from the suggestions under the box alike, so it grows as the browser is used rather than only when the search page is visited. A remembered subject reads like the row it came from - its glyph in its type's colour, its meaning beside it - and a remembered search keeps the clock icon, so the two kinds of row are told apart at a glance. Entries are kept by where they lead rather than by what they say, because 水 the kanji and 水 the word are one character and two pages, and keying on the character would have quietly dropped whichever was opened first. It is one store behind one key, so the header dropdown, the phone sheet and the results page are three views of the same history.

name: A way back out of the results
summary: Arrowing down through the results was a one-way trip. The list loads the next stretch as you approach the end, so it grows under you: forty rows into 中 the search box was far off the top of the screen, and the only route back was pressing up forty times - and overshooting downward on the way loaded more rows to climb. Nothing was looping, but nothing was leading out either, which reads the same from the keyboard. Escape now returns to the box from any row, and Home goes to the first row and then out to the box, both in a single press. Coming back also scrolls the box into view, which it did not before: the results scroll inside their own card on a page that scrolls too, so focus could land on a box still hidden above the results and typing went somewhere nobody could see.

name: Put explorer filters in the address
summary: Choosing N5 on the JLPT explorer changed nothing about the URL, so a filtered view could not be linked, bookmarked or reloaded. The level and study explorers had already put their filters in the address when they became real routes; this one had not followed. Its levels, WaniKani filter, level and grade filters and the sticky toggle are now written to the address as they change and read back on arrival, where the address wins over what the browser remembers - so a link to N5 opens on N5 whatever the last visit chose. A filter at its default says nothing, so a plain link stays plain.

name: A list is one surface, not forty boxes
summary: Three things a member could not do, all of them about lists. A list you saved yourself offered rename, edit characters, delete and practise, so the one thing you could not do with it was read it - the card's wall of glyphs was the whole view, with no meanings, no readings and no way into the glyph viewer. It opens now, into the same panel the Trouble and Favourites lists have always used, and the characters on the card open it as well as the Open action beside them. Bulk selection was reachable in the grid, where every card carries a checkbox, and unreachable in the list, where a row had none and clicking one opened the review modal instead of picking it - so a set could be gathered in one density and not the other, and Save to list sat above a list it could not be fed from. Rows carry the same checkbox now, and the same shift-click range. And the explorers drew their lists as forty bordered boxes stacked with gaps, each one an edge for the eye to stop at, while Study and History drew one surface with hairlines between the rows. Grades, the WaniKani library and the JLPT explorer take that chrome from the same place now.

name: Say whose work it is
summary: Four sources are borrowed here and three of them were credited. Tatoeba's sentences named Tatoeba, the stroke drawings named KanjiVG, the dictionary facts named KANJIDIC2 - each drawing its own paragraph, in its own file, with its own idea of what an external link should do. The meanings, the readings and the mnemonics are WaniKani's, they are by far the largest borrowing of the four, and they named nobody. They do now, on the vocabulary and radical pages and in the explorer's detail panel, and the four paragraphs are one component - so the next surface that shows borrowed content credits it by using the thing that draws it rather than by somebody remembering to. A source under its own terms rather than a public licence names no licence, and is not made to look as though it granted one. The credit itself moved out of the sentence loader on the way, which is server-only: a client component that wanted the Tatoeba credit was dragging the database client into the browser bundle.

name: Results in columns, with filters
summary: Search answered with one ranked column and a pill on every row saying which catalogue it came from. That is right and it is not enough: four catalogues answer a common character at once and they answer different questions - WaniKani knows what you are learning it as, the school grades know when a child is taught it, the dictionary knows the characters nobody teaches - and interleaving them by score left the reader sorting that out row by row from a pill. They sit side by side now, one column each, so a catalogue's whole answer reads or is ignored in a glance, and a column that found more than it shows opens on its own. Above them is a filter row on both axes, because the results have two and neither answers the other's question: what kind of thing a row is decides whether it is worth reading, and which catalogue holds it decides which column it sits in. A chip that is off keeps its count, so a hidden kind reads as hidden rather than as absent, and turning the last one off turns everything back on rather than leaving a page with nothing on it. The filters ride in the address, so a narrowed search can be sent to somebody and the back button walks them. The arrows learned the shape: up and down walk a column, left and right cross between them, keeping the row where the next column is long enough and clamping to its last row where it is not - WaniKani answers 中 with forty-five rows and the school grades with one, so every sideways move is between lists of different sizes and a move that landed on nothing would read as the keyboard being broken.

name: A digit is a number
summary: Searching for 1 found nothing at all. Not a near miss - nothing: the catalogues hold 一 and the meaning One, and neither of them contains the character 1, so a search that matches substrings of characters, readings and meanings had nothing to match against. Typing a digit is a reasonable way to ask for a number and every dictionary a learner has used answers it. A digit now reaches the number it names: 1 finds 一 and One, 10 finds 十, 24 finds 二十四, and a digit inside a phrase is read too, so 2 people reaches 二. The round ones are offered both ways, spelled out and bare - ten thousand is written 一万 but the character somebody typing 10000 wants is 万. A full-width digit reads the same, since that is what a Japanese keyboard produces. Above eight figures it offers nothing rather than a long spelling that would match nothing, and a query with no digits in it is left exactly as it was.

name: One list component, columns per page
summary: Every list of characters here shows a different set of fields, and always did: the study queue has an SRS stage, the grade explorer has on and kun readings and no SRS at all, the JLPT explorer has a school grade and an N level. What went wrong was letting that difference decide the layout too, so five surfaces grew five sets of row markup and five ideas of where a reading goes. A list declares its columns now - a heading, a lane width, and how to draw one cell - and the shared component owns everything else: the single surface with hairlines between rows, the aligned lanes, a heading row that cannot drift from the cells beneath it because both read the same widths, the checkbox, the row button, the leading and trailing slots, and what folds away on a phone. The grade explorer shows item, meaning, on, kun, strokes and JLPT; the JLPT explorer shows item, reading, meaning, grade, JLPT, status and SRS; the study queue and history keep the WaniKani six. Different fields, one shape. The explorers' detail panel opens under the row that was clicked through a slot of its own, which was the last thing about their lists that no column could express and the reason each had kept private row markup for so long.

name: Map viewer and study page
summary: The Map game held every prefecture's shape and a page of facts about it, and showed them one question at a time. The new Map page, under Explore, lays the same data out to be read. A large map fills the page; every region highlights under the pointer or a finger and says its name, and choosing one puts everything known about it beside the map - its name in its own script, its capital, size and population, what it is called, what it is number one for, its food, landmarks, symbols, emblem and history, and for a prefecture the kanji it is written with, each linking to its own page. On a phone the facts come up over the map instead. A country picker switches between Japan, the United States and Canada. The country and the chosen region ride in the address, so a page about Tokyo can be sent to somebody and opens on Tokyo, and the back button walks the choices. Requested 2026-09-01.

name: The word page gets its neighbourhood
summary: A word page listed the kanji it was written with and stopped - a dead end with two chips on it. It now goes on to the other words built from those same kanji, easiest first, so a page about one word is a way into its surroundings. Two sources could have supplied the list: each kanji's JLPT word examples cover more characters, but an example is only a string, with no level and no page unless the catalogue happens to hold it; each kanji's WaniKani words are catalogue rows with a level and an address, and every one of them has a page. The neighbourhood is drawn from the WaniKani words, because a list of places to go beats a longer list of names.

name: The kanji page knows what the study viewer knows
summary: Every search result lands on a kanji's own page, and that page knew less about the character than the study viewer behind the sign-in wall. It had the strokes, the dictionary facts and the sentences; it had no compounds, no radicals, no look-alikes, no vocabulary and no mnemonics - and the compounds are the reason anyone looks a kanji up. It has all of them now, and it is built as an ordered list of blocks, each fed by exactly one source and each drawing nothing when it has nothing. The layering is the decision that shaped it: the dictionary sources are the root and WaniKani is the bonus. KANJIDIC answers for all ten thousand characters, the JLPT table adds the words for the two thousand the exams cover, and WaniKani adds its radicals, look-alikes, vocabulary and mnemonics for the two thousand it teaches. A character WaniKani has never heard of gets a complete page; one it teaches gets a better one. The word inside a compound is not a link - most are not WaniKani vocabulary and would land on a page saying nothing is there - but every kanji inside it is, and every chip goes through the same address function the search results use, so following a result and following a chip land in the same place. The word and radical pages took the same blocks on the way, so a related chip or a mnemonic reads the same on all three. The page stays the same for every reader: a member's own study state is a block for a later release, not a reason to make a shareable address vary by who opens it.

name: One foot for every credit
summary: Every section of a subject page names where its content came from, and each named it a different way: the stroke-order panel with a rule across the full width and a small centred line beneath it, the dictionary facts with a left-aligned line at another size, the compounds and the relations and the mnemonics each at their own indent. Five cards down a page, five feet. The stroke-order foot was the right one and is now the only one. The credit component draws it, the block shell places it at the foot of the card with the rule running edge to edge, and every section that shows borrowed content sits on that shell - sentences, dictionary facts, the word and radical header, the stroke-order panel itself, which had been drawing its own copy of the style it inspired. The stroke animation alone keeps an inline line, because it draws inside another surface and has no edge of its own to put a rule on.

name: A page for every source, and what we hold from it
summary: Every credit on the site linked straight out to its vendor, which answered who and nothing else. Each one now leads first to a page of ours about that source: what we hold from it in numbers, when it was last brought in and how long ago that is in words, which release of theirs it came from where they publish one, what we take and under what terms, and only then the way out. Six sources have a page - WaniKani, KANJIDIC2, KanjiVG, kanjiapi.dev, Tatoeba and the school curriculum tables - each a tab away from the others, with an overview reachable from the footer. The three that live in the database stamp their own imports; the three built into the site as files say which upstream version they were built from. A credit is addressed by a key now rather than by an object, so a new source is one registry entry, one description and one page that already exists.

name: On and kun, labelled in Japanese
summary: The reading labels said On readings and Kun readings in English and nothing else, so a student asked about on'yomi on a test had never met the word here. Every label now carries the Japanese beside it - 音読み, 訓読み, 名乗り - with the romaji in a hover title. The readings under each are written the way a dictionary writes them, on in katakana and kun in hiragana, whichever way the source stored them: KANJIDIC had it right, the school tables sometimes did not, WaniKani never did, and one conversion now settles it for every page. Where there is room the romaji sits beside each reading in a lighter weight, for the reader still weak in kana, and steps aside on a phone. One component draws the line - the dictionary block, the grade cards, the grade list's two lanes, the JLPT detail and the stroke-order header all take it - so the label cannot be spelled two ways and the script cannot differ between pages.

name: The timeline is the ticket board
summary: Several agents work this repository at once, in sessions that cannot see each other, and requests were being tracked in the chat that received them - which is how a fix could ship for something nobody had written down, and how two sessions could build the same thing. The timeline JSON was already the one file they all read, so it is now the board. Every request, bug or idea goes in before the work starts, through pnpm backlog add, which takes a free ordering number, today's Vancouver date and the file's own escaping - the three things that went wrong when the file was edited by hand. An agent claims an entry before building it and puts it down if it stops; a claim cannot be taken over, only released. pnpm backlog prints what is open, what is in progress and who holds it, and how many are bugs, because a bug and a feature now say which they are. The admin release page shows the same claim and the same bug flag on each planned row. The rule is written into the agent instructions, so it holds for the next session as well as this one.

name: Stroke order in the faces a learner meets
summary: The stroke-order panel showed the character in two faces, Gothic and Mincho, each captioned in capitals underneath, and the captions drew the eye from the shapes. They are gone; the face's name is a hover title now. Two more faces join them, the two a learner actually meets: the textbook face (kyoukashotai), the handwriting standard every Japanese school teaches from and the one to copy where a printed form and the written form part ways, and a brush face the printed forms descend from. Neither ships with any system, so both come from Google Fonts at runtime, swapped in when they arrive. The four sit in a two-by-two grid beside the drawing, printed faces above and written faces beneath, and the stroke count pill has moved to the right of the header. Requested 2026-09-01.

name: The planned tab shows its queue out of order
summary: The admin release page sorted planned work by its place in the queue and then grouped it by the month of its estimated date, so the headers read September, August, September and the list looked as though it had lost its order. The estimates are typed by hand and mean little - one sat on a day that had already passed. A queue is not a calendar. The planned tab is one list now, in queue order, with each item's position shown where a release shows its version; the month grouping stays for what has shipped, where the date is a fact.

name: Winter Reading Challenge
summary: Hanako and Kamiko keep reading. The Winter Reading Challenge runs from 1 September to 6 December 2026, fourteen weeks, the Sunday of the week John named as the end. It was made from the July campaign the way the July one was made from the spring one, by hand at the time: the same thresholds, bonuses and streak, the weekly caps held flat at July's final week for every week of the window, the target their sum, the adults' opt-outs carried over so the leaderboard shows the same people, and the girls' books carried over so a book started in July can be checked in tomorrow. The July campaign is marked completed, which is what the site does itself when a new one activates. The making is a script now - pnpm campaign:create - that validates with the editor's own schema, snapshots every table it touches before writing, and does the whole change in one transaction, so the next campaign is made the same way rather than a slightly different way.

name: The open user menu renders under the list's sticky heading
summary: With the account menu open on a page showing a list, the list's sticky column headings drew straight across it. The panel itself sat at a layer nothing should beat, but its wrapper carried a small z-index of its own, and a wrapper with any z-index starts a stacking context - so the panel's layer only ordered it against its siblings, and against the page the whole menu was worth ten while a heading was worth twenty. The wrapper takes a named layer now, above page chrome and below the sheets and modals that must cover the header, and a test checks it against every sticky heading a list can draw.

name: Lists at the top level; Admin only in the menu
summary: Lists lived under Explore, which is where you go to find things; a list is something you made and come back to, and it was two clicks from everywhere. It is a destination of its own in the header now. Admin went the other way: it is a workspace rather than a place a member studies, so it has left the header row - which is now the same for everyone - and appears once in the account menu, for admins. The menu used to repeat every admin page, eleven entries, which was a second copy of the admin workspace's own tab row; the workspace is one click away and its tab row is the registry.

name: A new Google sign-in lands on the invite-code page
summary: Signing in with Google for the first time, with the site open to anyone, landed on Join with invite code - with no code, no way in and no way out but Sign out, and a refresh brought it straight back. The home page, the sign-in screen and the invite form itself each sent a signed-in viewer with no account to the invite form, while the page that actually creates an account was reachable only by typing its address. One rule now decides where such a viewer goes: the account page while signup is open, the invite form only when it is invite only. The invite form applies the rule too, so a newcomer cannot be shown it while the door is open, on arrival or on a refresh. Reported 2026-09-01 by John, signed in as a second Google account.

name: Winter campaign maxes at ¥40,000
summary: The Winter Reading Challenge was made by carrying the July campaign's final weekly cap across fourteen weeks, which came to a ¥96,000 base - far more than the ¥40,000 the family had in mind. The campaign is repriced: the ¥40,000 is spread flat across its fourteen weeks in tens of yen, the rounding paid in the final week so a perfect reader reaches the target on the goal date exactly, and the bonus caps keep July's proportion of bonus to base so a great week is still worth more than a good one. The campaign scripts now size the caps to a decided target rather than only printing it, and a reprice script changes both for a campaign already running.

name: Add to lists from search
summary: Searching ten kanji and keeping each one meant, for every kanji: open it, find the tag on its page, go back, search the next. The results dropdown and the search page now carry an Add to lists control at the edge of the list. Opened, every row grows a quiet column: the trouble and favourite marks the explorers use, then one small chip per saved list, lit when the row is already on it and toggled with a tap. The dropdown widens to make room; in the narrower search columns and on a phone the column drops to a line under the row. Kanji the JLPT and school-grade catalogues answer with borrow their WaniKani twin's id so they can be tagged too, and a word contributes its kanji to a list rather than its kana. Whether the column is open is remembered per browser. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Add to lists does not widen the dropdown
summary: Pressing Add to lists opened the filing column in the rows, but the dropdown kept its width, so on a desktop the chips were crushed against the meaning instead of sitting in a column on the right. The box that widens and the list that shows the column each kept their own copy of the open flag, and nothing told the box. One flag now, held once, with everything that shows it subscribed - flip it anywhere and the box and the rows change together. The cell sits inline only from the width where the box is truly wide; below that it drops to a line under the row, as on a phone. Reported 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Lists hold every kind of item
summary: A list was a string of characters, which is why it could only hold kanji and why a word added from search became its kanji. A list holds items now, each with its kind - radical, kanji, word, sentence - named the way its own catalogue names it, with WaniKani's id beside it where there is one, so a kanji WaniKani does not teach is still an item. A card previews words whole and shows kind chips; the viewer filters by kind; the editor takes kanji and words typed or pasted, reading a run of kanji one by one and anything with kana as a word; the search filer files a word as a word. The Lists page searches, sorts by last change, name or size, and reverses. Production's two lists were copied into items with a snapshot first, item for item. The base for every sharing feature; the first of the lists programme.

name: Public and private lists, with a link to share
summary: A list is a first-class thing, so it has an address of its own: /users/<member>/lists/<name>, the name in kebab case, a Japanese name kept as itself. The owner chooses Private, Link only or Public from the page. Link only makes an unguessable key the moment it is chosen, and the copy button hands out the link; Public needs no key. Whoever may open the list gets the same page - the name, who made it, when it was made and last changed, how often it has been shared, kind chips, a search, cards or rows - and somebody not signed in gets one quiet card inviting them to sign in and keep it. A private list reads as absent to everyone else. Names are displayable - letters in any script, digits and a title's punctuation, stray marks dropped - and two names that would share an address are refused. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Copy or subscribe to a list you are viewing
summary: Reading somebody's list now offers two ways to keep it, for two different promises. Copy makes a list of your own from its items - named so it fits on your shelf, Week 1 (copy) if you have a Week 1 - and remembers where it came from, while the source counts one more copy. Follow keeps the owner's list as theirs: read-only, always current, listed under Following on your Lists page with the owner's name, and dropped from there. A list made private since you followed it says so. The add-to-lists column from search sits on the list page as well, so one row of a friend's list can be tagged or filed into a list of your own. Both need exactly the permission that opening the list needs. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Open lists, locks and proposals
summary: A shared list can be opened so anyone who can see it adds to it at once, or kept locked, from a control beside the visibility. On a locked list a member's addition becomes a suggestion, typed into a box on the list's page with a note on why; taking an item out is always a suggestion, whoever asks, since a list open to additions is not open to being emptied. The owner sees the suggestions on the list itself - the item, the verb, who asked, when and why - and approves or declines each one; approving changes the list on the spot, and a suggestion that would decide nothing is never made. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Archive a list instead of deleting it
summary: A private list nobody else has seen is deleted, as it always was. A list that others hold - shared by link or public, followed, copied, or with suggestions waiting - is archived instead: closed to change for everyone, the owner included, still readable, copyable and followable by everyone who had it, and listed under Archived on the owner's Lists page with Restore and Delete for good. The confirmation says which of the two will happen before the click, and deleting for good says who loses the link. A follower whose list has gone private or away sees so on their own page. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: See who knows what across a shared list
summary: On a shared list, each member's standing on every item - not started, learning, known - as a small overlay, so a family can see who has the week's kanji down and who needs a hand. Uses each member's existing visibility setting. Suggested 2026-09-01.

name: Live system lists
summary: Seventy-two lists nobody owns, gathered at /lists: every JLPT level N5 to N1, every Japanese school grade and the junior-high set, and every one of WaniKani's sixty levels. They are not snapshots but live - a question stored as a list rather than rows, asked again each time one is opened - so Grade 1 is whatever the grade table says today and a WaniKani level is what it teaches now, radicals then kanji then the words that use them. Each has a public page of its own with the same rows, kind chips, search and burned filter a member's list gets, and the two ways to keep it: follow it and it stays current under Lists that keep themselves on your own page, or copy it and it becomes rows of your own, to cut down to half of Grade 1 or to Grade 1 without what you already know. The index sits under Explore as Kanji lists. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: A note on an item in a list
summary: Why this item is here: a short note per item, written by whoever added it - a mnemonic, the sentence it was met in, the mistake it keeps causing. Shown in the list and when practising from it. Suggested 2026-09-01.

name: Pull updates into a copied list
summary: A copied list remembers its source and can pull what has been added there since, item by item, so a copy taken from a friend's growing list does not fall behind without becoming a subscription. Suggested 2026-09-01.

name: Build a list from pasted text
summary: Paste a passage, a handout or a page of a book into the Lists page and every word the catalogue knows and every kanji in the text comes out, words matched longest-first so a run reads as the words it holds rather than a string of characters. What comes out is a preview to massage before anything is written: each item is a button that takes itself out, a whole kind can be dropped at once, and the list is saved only when it is named. Pasted text is treated as hostile - cut to a cap of twenty thousand characters, stripped of control characters, never stored, never rendered as anything but the words in the box, and answered only with items the catalogue already knew, so markup or SQL in a paste comes back as nothing at all. Requested 2026-09-01 by John, restated 2026-09-02 with the safety and massage requirements.

name: Practise and review from any list you can see
summary: Every game and practice mode that takes a list takes a subscribed or shared one too, so a list a friend shares is something to play, not only to read. Suggested 2026-09-01.

name: A burn list that hides what you know
summary: A third built-in list beside Trouble and Favourites: Burned, for the items you know so well you never need to read them again. It starts empty for everyone, and is marked by hand with a third mark - a small flame - on every glyph the other two marks are on. A member with WaniKani connected opens the Burned list and sees an offer with the count on it, Apply 157 burned from WaniKani, applied on the click and again whenever they like, never silently on sync. Applied, a Hide burned toggle on the list viewer and on every list page takes those items out and says how many went, so a list never looks shorter than it is without saying why. There is no practice sheet for what you know. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Every list surface: sortable, pageable, searchable, fast
summary: Lists, like all data on the site, are sortable, reversible, pageable, scrollable, searchable, cached and fast. The Lists page and the list viewer get search, sort by name, size and last change, and paging once a list outgrows a screen; the same standard applies to every surface that lists data. Stated 2026-09-01 by John as a standing rule.

name: What a list says about itself
summary: Every list carries the facts a reader wants before opening it: when it was made, when it last changed, who made it, how many hold it, how many times it has been copied and shared. Shown on the card and on the public view. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Browse kanji by stroke count
summary: A stroke browser beside the WaniKani levels and the school grades: the counts 1 to N as chips, and choosing one shows every kanji with that many strokes, with the same cards, rows, tags, selection and add-to-lists as the other explorers. The dictionary already knows each kanji's stroke count. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Mark a list studied, and grade it
summary: A list can be marked complete or studied by its owner, and carries a grade the system assigns after a study or review pass over it - how much of the list is known, and how well it went. Shown on the card and the list's page. Ties to practising from a list and the who-knows-what overlay. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Print a list from the lists page
summary: Every list card and list page has a Print action that opens the list as a sheet: the items with meanings and readings, or the tracing sheet the practice pages already print, chosen at the click. Requested 2026-09-01 by John.

name: Merge lists
summary: Two or more of your lists made into one, from the Lists page. They are numbered as they are picked, because the order is the answer - merging Week 1 and Week 2 should read as Week 1 then Week 2 - and the panel says how big the result will be and how many items the lists shared before anything is written. Clearing the sources away afterwards is a choice rather than the default, and goes through the same rule the delete button uses, so a source somebody else follows is archived rather than deleted out from under them. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: The list viewer edits, resets and says what it is
summary: Three things John found opening his own lists. Opening a saved list offered Choose and no way to take an item out - the remove button the Trouble and Favourites lists always had now works on a saved list too, in place. Choosing was remembered across lists, so closing one list and opening another opened it still choosing, with the first list's picks counted; choosing resets when a different list opens. And the viewer's title was the bare name with a '10 items' pill in the toolbar, so nothing said this was a saved list: the title now says Saved list above the name and carries the count beside it, and the search box has a clear button and offers the list's own items as they are typed, like the other search boxes. Reported 2026-09-02 by John.

name: Quiet rows, an edit mode, and romaji in lists
summary: Three things reported together. The search page had become unreadable: every row carried a kind pill, a level pill, a Strokes chip and - because the filing column had been opened once and was remembered for ever - two tag marks and a chip per list. Filing is now held for the sitting rather than the browser, so it is off unless it was opened in this tab, and the Strokes chip is gone, since the kanji page a row already leads to opens the same animation in the same number of clicks. The Burned list's offer to apply WaniKani's burned items counted every burned item rather than the ones not applied yet, so it still said Apply 1,728 after applying them; it counts what is left and disappears at zero. Removing an item from a list showed a mark on every card with no mode to explain it, and is now behind an Edit toggle in the viewer. And searching inside a list read the raw string, so water found 水 and mizu found nothing while the search box on the same page found both: both list surfaces now read a query the way search does, romaji turned to kana and tried against the readings. Reported 2026-09-02 by John with screenshots.

name: Map insets collide with the mainland
summary: On Japan, Okinawa's inset box overlaps Kagoshima, so the two are read as one place; move the inset clear of the mainland, to the right or into empty space. On the United States, Alaska sits too near the left edge and Hawaii needs a home of its own: Alaska above, Hawaii below. Reported 2026-09-02 by John with screenshots.

name: RESTful URLs across the site
summary: Addresses should read as paths rather than query strings: the map is /map?region=21 for Gifu and should be /study/maps/japan/gifu or /japan/21. No compatibility redirects and no fake paths - breaking old URLs is fine. Applies site-wide, not only to the map. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: Every list under Lists, and one search field
summary: The auto lists sat under Explore as Kanji lists while a member's own lists sat under Lists, on a page that looked nothing like theirs. Every list lives under Lists now: the built-in two, the sets you saved, the lists you follow, the auto lists in full - all of them on one page, in sections, with a star on the auto lists you follow. Explore has lost its Kanji lists entry, and Lists leads a visitor with no page of their own to the auto lists, which are the part of Lists that belongs to everybody. The three list surfaces also shared out one search field, so the viewer, a list's page and an auto list's page all clear with an X and offer the list's own items as you type, rather than one having both and two having neither. They are called Auto lists now, which is what John called them. Requested 2026-09-02 by John with screenshots.

name: Searching an English meaning misses the kanji
summary: Searching Morning returns the word and the radical but never the kanji it names, so the one thing a learner asked for is the one thing missing. Reported 2026-09-02 by John.

name: Add to lists wherever a kanji is shown
summary: The filing column exists only on the search surfaces. A member who searches a kanji, opens its page and wants it on a list has no way to do it. Every page and panel that shows a kanji, word or radical - the subject pages, the glyph viewer, the explorers - offers the same tag marks and list chips. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: Convert money in search
summary: Typing 14.40 CAD or 23 EUR answers with the amount in yen, and a yen amount answers in the other direction. Needs a rate source that will not throttle. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: Read large Japanese numbers in search
summary: A number written the Japanese way - 一億二千万 - answers with the English number, and the reverse. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: Convert Japanese era years in search
summary: Typing Heisei 3, Showa 40 or 令和6年 answers with the Western year and the era in kanji, as its own line of results. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: One view of a list, not a modal and a page
summary: A list opened as a panel from one control and as a page from another, so which view a member got was a mystery, and the two had drifted apart. There is one view now, and it is the page. Trouble, Favourites and Burned have addresses of their own - /users/<member>/lists/trouble and its two siblings - and every card, name and button leads to a page. The panel is gone, and nothing went with it: the page draws the same subject cards and rows every other surface uses, with the member's own SRS state and tags on them, and it carries choosing and the practice sheet, the glyph viewer, an Edit toggle that takes an item out - untagging a built-in list, dropping a row from a saved one - and the WaniKani offer on Burned. Opening somebody else's list shows how far you have got with what is on it, since the state read is the reader's own. Reported 2026-09-02 by John.

name: The JLPT explorer errors for a member with no WaniKani
summary: Opening the JLPT explorer as an account with no WaniKani connection answered We could not load this user drilldown. The page asked WaniKani for the member's own kanji with an empty token, took a 401 and threw, so the one page that is a table of every JLPT kanji - the part of the site that needs WaniKani least - was the one page a member without WaniKani could not open. It asks only when there is a connection to ask with, and a token that has since been revoked is treated the same way: the explorer opens, and the member's own progress is simply the part that is not there. Reported 2026-09-02 by John.

name: An Internal kind of member, for Read
summary: The Read tab and the reading check-ins are the family's, not the public's. A member is one of three kinds - admin, internal, everyone else - and Read is offered only to the first two. The members who have been here a month with WaniKani count as internal. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: The school grades search has no autocomplete
summary: Every other search offers what it holds as you type; the grades page does not. Reported 2026-09-02 by John.

name: The profile says Not connected and offers no way to connect
summary: A new member's profile shows WaniKani Not connected with no link to connect one or to edit the token. Reported 2026-09-02 by John.

name: The JLPT form is open before anybody asks for it
summary: The profile shows the member's JLPT level and then the form to change it, always open. A member may hold several certificates, so the profile lists what they have reported and offers Add another or Change; the form appears when it is asked for. The Display section could be condensed while we are there. Reported 2026-09-02 by John.

name: One control for the text inside item pills
summary: The pills that stand for a kanji or a word turn up in several places - the words a kanji is used in, the related groups on a subject page, a paste being turned into a list, a list being edited - and they had drifted: some carried the reading and the meaning, some carried the glyph alone. They are one component now, and every one of them can say what it is: the reading and the meaning under the glyph, with one control that shows or hides that text everywhere at once, remembered per browser and on by default. The paste preview gained the words it was missing, so a chapter comes back as items a member can read rather than a wall of characters to guess at. The pill also decides for itself what is Japanese, so a radical WaniKani draws by name is no longer set in a Japanese face. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: Explore becomes Learn, Map becomes Maps
summary: The header group called Explore is where a member goes to learn - the two explorers, the school grades, the practice sheets, the maps - so it is called Learn. The maps entry is called Maps, since there are three countries behind it and more to come, and the page names itself the same way. Requested 2026-09-02 by John.

name: Logout does not log you out
summary: Pressing Sign out in the account menu led to a page with Logout and Join as tabs above it and Cancel beside the button, so a member who had asked to leave was still signed in and had no way to tell from looking. The menu signs you out there and then and lands on the home page. It is a button rather than a link, because a link to a page that ends a session would be prefetched on hover and hovering a menu must not sign anybody out. The page itself is still there for anybody who arrives at it directly, without the two tabs, and it says plainly that you are still signed in until you press the button. Reported 2026-09-02 by John.
